transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-30
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Lena (Orion Lead ML Eng), Dr. Samir (CTO), Priya (SRE)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on KV cache behavior Orion is seeing in private deployment: frequent evictions during long-context sessions, observed paging to CPU and spikes in latency when prefix reuse patterns change. Goal: root cause and propose config changes + repro plan and pilot.

Topics:
- KV cache eviction policy (LRU vs segmented)
- Paging to host memory / CPU fallback
- Prefix reuse causing fragmentation and cache churn
- Long-context sessions and batch sizing
- Quantization impacts on memory footprint
- VPC/on-prem constraints and observability gaps

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll go about an hour. Jonah and I will lead, we wanted to get into the KV cache evictions you reported. 
[00:18] Lena: yeah thanks, uh we started seeing these evictions after onboarding the 70k token contexts. basically sessions that are long, with lots of prompt history, we see intermittent latency spikes and some generation failures.
[00:32] Jonah: okay k, can you give a concrete example of a request that triggers it? like sequence lengths, batch sizes?
[00:40] Lena: sure, typical user flows hit around 45k tokens, sometimes 70k when they include attachment transcripts. Batches are small, usually 1-4 concurrent, but prefixes are highly reused — same 2-3 system prompts + user history. 
[00:55] Dr. Samir: to add, it's on our private deployment in our VPC on-prem. We cannot offload to hosted. And we've pinned the model to redwood-llm-v2-8b-quant.
[01:11] Jonah: that helps. So you're on a quantized 8B — interesting. Two immediate things: (1) quant reduces model weights but KV memory grows with sequence length and kv entries regardless of weight quant. (2) prefix reuse can cause cold vs hot segments in the cache.
[01:27] Priya: we're seeing OOMs on the infer nodes then the pods restart; sometimes we see paging where GPU memory seems to be evicted and host memory usage shoots up.
[01:35] Maya: okay, sounds like KV eviction + paging interplay. Jonah, can you explain how KV is laid out in the runtime?
[01:44] Jonah: sure — high level, we maintain KV shards per layer on GPU; for long contexts we chunk the sequence into segments, we keep active KV for recent tokens in fast LRU-style caches and older segments can be paged out to host or disk depending on configured paging policies. In private deployments paging defaults to host RAM unless the admin enabled NVMe swap.
[02:05] Lena: are the evictions strictly LRU? we thought we saw evictions even for recently used prefixes when concurrency spikes.
[02:12] Jonah: LRU is the baseline but we also have a segmentation policy: each segment has its own LRU window, and we do global eviction when total KV exceed threshold. Under bursts, the global eviction can evict segments that still have hot prefixes if the segment budget is full — leads to what looks like evicting recently used tokens.
[02:32] Dr. Samir: so prefix reuse could actually make things worse if reuse is concentrated in a few segments?
[02:36] Jonah: exactly — if many sessions use the same prefix but the prefix spans many different sequences, the cache may store duplicated KV entries across shards, increasing pressure. That duplication plus chunking boundaries can cause fragmentation.
[02:49] Maya: is there de-duplication for identical prefixes across requests?
[02:52] Jonah: we do some prefix dedupe on the controller side for hosted offering; in private deployments we rely on the customer's routing and, in older runtime versions, dedupe wasn't enabled by default. It's configurable.
[03:05] Priya: we are on runtime v3.1.0 — is that too old?
[03:09] Jonah: v3.1.0 predates the more aggressive dedup and segmented eviction heuristics we shipped in v3.3.0. I'd expect enabling dedupe and bumping to v3.4.1 to help.
[03:22] Lena: hmm we tried upgrading once but had kernel driver mismatches on the nodes. We wanted to avoid a full cluster upgrade.
[03:28] Maya: understood — we can help with a staged upgrade and compatibility checklist. In the meantime, any config changes you can try that don't require a full runtime upgrade?
[03:36] Jonah: yes, two quick levers: increase the per-pod KV budget (if you have spare GPU HBM), and tune the global eviction threshold to prefer segment-level LRU instead of global aggressive eviction. Also enable short TTL for rarely used segments so they get paged earlier rather than causing sudden large evictions.
[03:56] Dr. Samir: what's the risk with bumping per-pod budget? we have high contention — could that starve other pods?
[04:03] Jonah: it can, if GPU HBM is limited. That's why this needs a coordinated plan: either increment budgets on a few inference pools, or isolate the long-context traffic to dedicated nodes (which is what Redwood Dedicated does) — isolating prevents cross-workload eviction.
[04:19] Lena: isolating traffic is appealing but we're on a constrained on-prem cluster. We can't spare dedicated nodes right now.
[04:24] Priya: plus network topology in our VPC prevents us from adding extra nodes easily.
[04:28] Maya: ok, let's cover software mitigations then. Jonah, what about paging — we saw paging to CPU which spiked latency. Any config to reduce host fallback?
[04:36] Jonah: you can disable automatic paging and instead fail fast when KV budget exceeded — that'll avoid huge latency spikes but will increase failure rates. Alternatively, configure NVMe-backed swap with async prefetching so evicted segments are still retrievable quickly; it's a trade between P99 latency and success rate.
[04:56] Dr. Samir: latency spikes are killing our SLA — users see 5-10s delays. Failing fast might be better than a 10s hang.
[05:03] Jonah: agree. Also, a small tweak: enable prefix coalescing at the router level — join identical prefixes so the runtime only materializes one copy. That can cut KV duplication substantially.
[05:15] Lena: is that safe for our multi-tenant flows? sometimes prompts include request-specific tokens.
[05:20] Jonah: coalescing only when the prefix fingerprint matches exactly; you can opt into deterministic hashing to avoid accidental collisions. We'll provide the fingerprinting guidance.
[05:29] Priya: ok what about batching? our bursts are small, but we see high token-per-request counts. Any batching advice?
[05:34] Jonah: continuous batching helps throughput but can worsen KV pressure because combined sequences can keep more KV live. For long-context, prefer micro-batching of similar sequence-lengths and cap maximum batch token sum. Also use dynamic batch windows so short requests don't wait.
[05:49] Maya: another factor mentioned was quantization — does quant help the KV problem?
[05:54] Jonah: quant lowers model weights, reducing model param memory, but KV memory is mostly float16 or cached kv format — quant doesn't proportionally reduce KV size. However, lighter models produce shorter KV footprints per token sometimes; it's workload dependent.
[06:09] Lena: we use 8-bit quant for weights; maybe we can try a smaller context model at times.
[06:13] Dr. Samir: are there telemetry gaps we should fill to diagnose? we saw only surface-level metrics.
[06:18] Jonah: yes, add per-segment KV resident bytes, per-shard eviction counters, PCIe transfer rates, and timeline of page-in/page-out events. Also collect request fingerprints and sequence length histograms. We'll share a metric dashboard JSON you can import.
[06:33] Priya: right now our logs only show 'eviction event' without why or which segment.
[06:39] Jonah: that’s the key — we need to correlate request fingerprints to eviction events and GPU memory pictures. Also capture OS-level RAM and DMA stats.
[06:47] Lena: can Redwood run a repro on your hosted infra so we can compare behavior?
[06:51] Maya: we can run a scoped repro on a dedicated pool if you're willing to share anonymized traces and sample prompts. We'll mirror your sequence lengths and prefix patterns.
[06:59] Dr. Samir: we can share sanitized traces. Concern: PII and data residency — we need an NDA and for logs to be scrubbed.
[07:06] Maya: understood; we'll use the redwood private pilot flow and sign a limited NDA. We'll also run in a customer-owned VPC option if you'd rather.
[07:14] Jonah: operationally, our repro will test: (a) segmenting policy change, (b) dedupe on/off, (c) paging mode (host vs nvme vs fail-fast), (d) per-pod KV budget changes. We'll capture evictions and latency.
[07:29] Lena: sounds good. for quick wins, which config should we try first?
[07:33] Jonah: enable prefix dedupe and increase per-pod KV budget 10% on the nodes handling long-context; set paging to fail-fast as a canary so we avoid long stalls. We'll also add per-segment TTL to force earlier paging of truly cold segments.
[07:48] Priya: are there any safety concerns with fail-fast? We might see more 5xxs which product won't like.
[07:53] Maya: tradeoff but we can route a small percent of traffic to the fail-fast pool for canary, then scale if stable.
[07:59] Dr. Samir: timeline for those steps?
[08:02] Jonah: we can provide a config patch and a k8s job to apply to a canary namespace — low risk. Should be doable in 48-72 hours.
[08:11] Lena: we'll get the traces to you by end of week.
[08:14] Maya: perfect — we'll also send the compatibility checklist for upgrading runtime to v3.4.1 and the dedupe toggle docs.
[08:21] Jonah: one more note on prefix reuse — if your prefixes include user-specific tokens that change frequently, dedupe won't help. You might consider canonicalizing prefixes server-side to move volatile tokens into the dynamic tail.
[08:34] Lena: oh interesting — we can try token masking on prefixes to increase reuse. We'll experiment.
[08:40] Priya: recording this as an action: we'll provision a canary namespace and allow Redwood to run the repro with sanitized traces.
[08:47] Maya: thanks. last question: any recommended observability dashboards for on-prem?
[08:52] Jonah: yes — GPU HBM utilization by shard, per-segment resident bytes, eviction rate per minute, host paging I/O, and request fingerprint map. We'll send a Grafana dashboard and a Prometheus scrape config.
[09:06] Dr. Samir: that covers it. thanks, team.
[09:10] Maya: recap / next steps: Jonah will run initial analysis and push config suggestions; Orion will share traces; we'll schedule a follow-up after repro.
[09:20] Lena: thanks all.

Notes: transcription contains some speaker label swaps and slight mistranscriptions (e.g., "K-V cash" vs KV cache). Action items recorded above.
